mastery.oneLine: An assessment system that uses how symptoms respond to repeated movements to guide a self-management exercise plan.
mastery.whatItIs: McKenzie Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy (MDT) is mostly active care. You test repeated movements or sustained positions, watch how pain moves, and use the response to classify the problem and choose exercises the patient does themselves.
mastery.analogy: Like a compass for movement: the pain's behavior points toward the direction that helps, rather than assuming one exercise suits everyone.
coreIdeas: Directional preference: some people improve with a repeated movement direction (often extension), others with flexion or sideways movements.
Centralization: pain moving from the leg toward the spine during testing is a good sign; peripheralization (moving away) is a warning.
The patient learns to manage symptoms themselves, with minimal dependence on hands-on treatment.

terms.meaning: Pain or symptoms moving from the limb back toward the spine.
Symptoms moving farther down the limb.
A movement direction that consistently reduces symptoms.
A pattern where repeated movements change symptom location and range.
Pain from tight tissue at end range, or from prolonged poor positions.

whenToUse: Back or neck pain, with or without arm or leg pain, with no red flags.
When you want the patient to take charge of treatment.
whenNot: Red flags: progressive weakness, loss of bowel or bladder control, saddle numbness, major trauma or systemic illness.
When symptoms peripheralize or neurological signs worsen during testing.

steps.title: Draw a symptom map
steps.detail: Record where symptoms are, which is the farthest, and daily-task limits.

steps.title: Screen
steps.detail: Rule out red flags and check neurological status.

steps.title: Test repeated movements
steps.detail: Example: repeated extension in lying for about 10 repetitions.

steps.title: Watch the response
steps.detail: Note location, intensity and after-effects. Does leg pain retreat toward the back?

steps.title: Classify and prescribe
steps.detail: If a direction helps, teach it as a home exercise; if not, test another.

steps.title: Review across visits
steps.detail: Recheck symptom map, function and neurological status.

mastery.dose: Typical teaching range: about 10 repetitions of the helpful movement, repeated several times a day while symptoms are active, adjusted by a trained clinician.

example.patient: Carlos, 41, driver, low back pain and calf pain after sitting.
example.assessment: Repeated extension in lying makes the calf pain retreat to the buttock; flexion makes it worse.
example.treatment: He is taught extension in lying, 10 repetitions every few hours, and posture advice for driving.
example.reassess: Calf pain is gone after a week and walking improves. If it had worsened or weakness appeared, the plan would change.

mistakes: Declaring a disc has been 'put back'.
mastery.recap: Follow the symptom response, not the famous exercise.
mastery.evidence: MDT has research as an assessment and self-management system, with benefits depending on the condition and comparison. Directional preference and centralization are recognized patterns, though they do not prove a disc moved.

depth.why: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy sorts patients by how symptoms respond to repeated movements or sustained positions. Centralisation (symptoms retreating toward the spine) or a directional preference points to a movement the patient can use as treatment; peripheralisation (symptoms spreading away) says that direction is wrong. Care is mostly active and patient-led, with education to prevent recurrence. The disc-displacement explanation is a model, not a proven mechanism; the clinical value is the structured response testing and the self-management it produces.
choose: Use it for spinal pain, especially with leg or arm symptoms, when movement changes the symptoms in a repeatable way.
Prefer another assessment when no movement or position changes the symptom pattern, or when pain is constant and unaffected by movement.
Choose it when the patient can understand and carry out frequent self-treatment between visits.
Add clinician overpressure only when the patient's own movement stops short of the response.
parameters: Repeated movements (commonly 10-15 repetitions) or sustained positions in one direction, noting where symptoms are during and after
Symptoms retreating toward the spine are a good sign even if the back is briefly worse; spreading or worsening is a reason to stop that direction
Frequent, short self-treatment bouts through the day, often hourly at first, reduced as symptoms settle
Re-check the same movement and the symptom location at each visit before changing direction
depth.progress: Start with the direction that centralises or reduces symptoms, add overpressure or a progression only if the response stalls, then move to restoring function and to prevention exercises. As symptoms resolve, reduce the frequency and teach the patient to repeat the movement at the first sign of a recurrence.
measure: Symptom location (centralising, peripheralising or unchanged) recorded before, during and after each test
Pain intensity and range in the tested direction, measured the same way each visit
Function: sitting, walking or lifting tolerance, which shows whether the response carries over
depth.evidence: MDT has a substantial research base as an assessment and management system, and some trials support it in subgroups, especially patients who centralise. Results depend on the condition and the subgroup, so it is not established that any single exercise fixes every disc problem.
pitfalls: Testing too few repetitions or only one direction, then calling the test negative.
Ignoring peripheralisation and continuing a direction that spreads the symptoms.
Treating the method as a fixed exercise recipe instead of a response-driven process.
Taking over the movement for the patient instead of building self-management.
screen: Progressive weakness, bladder or bowel change, or saddle symptoms (urgent medical assessment)
Major trauma, suspected fracture, infection, or unexplained pain with a cancer history

intro.en: McKenzie sorts mechanical spine pain into three syndromes. Each is found with repeated movements and handled differently.
intro.ur: McKenzie mechanical spine pain ko teen syndromes mein baantta hai. Har ek repeated movements se dhoondi jati hai aur alag tareeqe se handle hoti hai.

tag.en: Pain moves toward the centre with one direction
tag.ur: Ek direction se dard center ki taraf

what.en: Pain changes with repeated movement, and one direction centralises it (pulls it toward the spine). That direction becomes the exercise.
what.ur: Repeated movement se dard badalta hai, aur ek direction use centralise karti hai (spine ki taraf khinchti hai). Wahi direction exercise ban jati hai.

en: Test repeated movements one direction at a time.
Find the direction that centralises or reduces the pain.
Repeat that direction often, with a plan to maintain posture.
ur: Repeated movements ek ek direction mein test karein.
Woh direction dhoondein jo dard ko centralise ya kam karti hai.
Wahi direction aksar dohrayein aur posture barqarar rakhne ka plan banayein.

tag.en: Pain only at the end of one movement
tag.ur: Sirf ek movement ke end par dard

what.en: Pain appears only when a shortened tissue is stretched at the end of range, and stops when the stretch is released.
what.ur: Dard tab aata hai jab chhota hua tissue range ke end par stretch hota hai, aur stretch chhorne par ruk jata hai.

en: Find the end-range movement that reproduces the pain.
Repeat that movement to the point of mild discomfort.
Do it often; the tissue remodels over weeks.
ur: Woh end-range movement dhoondein jo dard dohrati hai.
Halki takleef tak us movement ko dohrayein.
Aksar karein; tissue hafton mein remodel hota hai.

tag.ur: Der tak end position se dard

what.en: Pain only comes from holding an end position for a long time, and goes when the posture changes. Movements themselves are normal.
what.ur: Dard sirf ek end position der tak rakhne se aata hai, aur posture badalne par chala jata hai. Movements khud normal hoti hain.

en: Show the position that provokes the pain.
Correct the posture and the pain eases.
Teach regular breaks and posture changes.
ur: Woh position dikhayein jo dard paida karti hai.
Posture theek karein to dard kam hota hai.
Waqfa aur posture ki tabdeeli ki aadat sikhayein.

urdu.short: McKenzie MDT ek assessment aur self-management system hai jo repeated movements ya sustained positions ke baad symptoms ki tabdeeli dekh kar exercises choose karta hai. Har patient ko extension dena sahi nahi; response direction batata hai.

details.heading: Yeh kya hai?
details.text: MDT zyada tar active care hai. Clinician repeated movements ya sustained positions test karta hai, pain ki location aur response dekhta hai, phir pattern classify karke patient ko khud karne wali exercises sikhata hai.

details.heading: Misal se samjhein
details.text: Yeh movement ka compass hai: symptoms ka rawaiya us direction ki taraf ishara karta hai jo madad kare, bajaye is ke ke har shakhs ko ek hi exercise di jaye.

details.heading: Bunyadi ideas
details.text: Directional preference: kuch log repeated extension se behtar hote hain, kuch flexion ya side movement se. Centralization: test ke dauran limb ka dard spine ki taraf wapas aaye to yeh favorable response ho sakta hai. Peripheralization: symptoms limb mein aur door chale jayein to yeh warning hai. Patient ko self-management sikhana central feature hai.

details.heading: Aham terms
details.text: Centralization: symptoms limb se spine ki taraf move karna. Peripheralization: symptoms limb mein aur neeche ya door jana. Directional preference: woh movement direction jo consistently symptoms kam kare. Derangement: aisa pattern jahan repeated movements symptom location aur range badal sakte hain. Dysfunction/Postural: end-range par tight tissue ya lambi der ki posture se related pain ke patterns.

details.heading: Kab use karein / kab nahi
details.text: Red flags ke baghair back/neck pain, arm ya leg pain ke sath bhi, aur jab patient ko self-management dena maqsad ho. Progressive weakness, bowel/bladder control ka loss, saddle numbness, major trauma ya systemic illness mein urgent medical review chahiye. Testing se symptoms peripheralize hon ya neurological signs barhein to us direction ko continue na karein.

details.heading: Steps
details.text:
1. Symptom map banayein: jagah, sab se door symptom aur daily-task limits.
2. Red flags aur neurological status screen karein.
3. Repeated movements test karein; example ke taur par lying mein extension ke takreeban 10 reps.
4. Location, intensity aur baad ke effects note karein: kya leg pain back ki taraf retreat karta hai?
5. Helpful direction ho to home exercise sikhayein; warna doosri direction assess karein.
6. Visits ke darmiyan symptom map, function aur neurological status dobara check karein.

details.heading: Dose
details.text: Teaching mein helpful movement ke takreeban 10 reps din mein kai martaba diye ja sakte hain jab symptoms active hon, magar trained clinician response ke mutabiq adjust kare.

details.heading: Clinical example — source ka scenario
details.text: Source mein Carlos, 41 saal ke driver, ko sitting ke baad low-back aur calf pain hai. Lying mein repeated extension se calf pain buttock ki taraf retreat karta hai, jabke flexion se barhta hai. Use extension exercise aur driving posture advice sikhayi jati hai; follow-up mein calf pain khatam aur walking behtar hoti hai. Symptoms barhte ya weakness aati to plan badalta. Yeh teaching scenario hai, prescription nahi.

details.heading: Aam ghaltiyan
details.text: Har patient ko extension dena; symptoms peripheralize hone par bhi continue karna; ya kehna ke disc ko 'wapis jagah par' rakh diya gaya.

details.heading: Self-test
details.text: Centralization ka matlab? Symptoms spine ki taraf wapas aana. Kya extension sab ke liye sahi hai? Nahi, response faisla karta hai.

details.heading: Recap aur evidence
details.text: Mashhoor exercise ke bajaye symptom response follow karein. MDT ko assessment aur self-management system ke taur par research kiya gaya hai; faida condition aur comparison par depend karta hai. Directional preference ya centralization disc ki movement prove nahi karti.

deeper.heading: Clinical reasoning
deeper.text: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy (MDT), jise aksar McKenzie method kaha jata hai, repeated movements, sustained positions aur symptom response se classification aur self-management guide karta hai. Har patient ko extension ya aik fixed direction prescribe nahi hoti.

deeper.heading: Directional preference aur response
deeper.text: Assessment mein symptoms ka centralize, peripheralize, improve ya worsen hona observe kiya ja sakta hai. Repeated movement ka selection individual response aur safety screening par depend karta hai; symptoms spread ya neurological signs worsen hon to reassess karein.

deeper.heading: Common mistakes aur self-management
deeper.text: Sab low-back pain patients ko same exercise dena, symptom response record na karna aur red flags ignore karna avoid karein. Patient ko safe self-management aur clear stop/review guidance dein.

deeper.heading: Evidence aur limits
deeper.text: MDT selected spinal pain presentations mein useful framework ho sakta hai, magar har diagnosis ya patient ke liye superior nahi. Classification ko evolving clinical picture ke saath update karein aur exercise, education aur function ko central rakhein.

cue.wake: MDT is not a club where every member must do press-ups.
cue.question: The calf pain retreats toward the back during a trial. What should you track?
cue.answer: Symptom location, after-effects and function. Do not claim a disc was put back.
cue.easy: Centralization = pain or symptoms move away from the outer limb toward the spine.
cue.remember: Follow the symptom map, not the famous exercise.

worldDeep.opening: A man sits down and says, 'My sciatica has moved into the calf and apparently signed a long lease.' A repeated-movement assessment may change the location of symptoms—and suddenly this becomes a detective story about response patterns, not a competition to prescribe the most famous back extension. Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy (MDT) is an assessment, classification, education and self-management system associated with Robin McKenzie.

principles.title: Directional preference is discovered, not assigned
principles.body: The patient's response to a specific loading direction or sustained position may reveal clinically relevant improvement in symptoms, movement or function. It is not the clinician choosing extension in advance because that exercise has better publicity. Confirmation over follow-up is important.

principles.title: Centralization describes where symptoms move
principles.body: With appropriate spinal movement testing, distal symptoms can reduce or retreat proximally; that pattern is called centralization. Record changes in the most distal symptom carefully, including after-effects. Centralization can be clinically informative but does not diagnose which disc structure moved.

principles.title: Peripheralization is information, not a challenge to push harder
principles.body: When symptoms travel farther from the spine or neurologic findings worsen during a trial, stop and reassess. Movement should never be prescribed solely because the theoretical model predicts it ought to work.

principles.title: The major MDT classifications
principles.body: Derangement is defined through a characteristic directional preference/loading response; Dysfunction involves consistent limited-end-range or contractile loading responses; Postural involves symptoms from sustained static loading. 'Other' recognizes presentations that do not fit those patterns, including concerning pathology and mechanically inconclusive conditions.

principles.title: Self-management is a clinical objective
principles.body: The aim is not to make the patient dependent on repeated hands-on treatment. A tailored and tolerable movement plan, education about symptom behavior, and follow-up progressions give the patient ways to observe and manage the condition independently.

assessment.title: Behavioral history before a movement test
assessment.body: Map symptom location precisely: back, buttock, thigh, calf or foot; ask which symptom is most distal. Clarify pain trends, time course, positions, loading, sleep, neurological concerns, major trauma, bowel/bladder changes and the patient's target activity.

assessment.title: Repeated or sustained loading assessment
assessment.body: After screening, examine appropriate baseline motion and the response to carefully selected directions or positions. Record symptom location, intensity, range, quality and after-effects after a small supervised trial. Avoid assuming every patient can or should perform end-range repetitions.

assessment.title: Classify provisionally and revisit
assessment.body: Distinguish a directional-preference pattern from consistent end-range pain, sustained postural loading, and nonmechanical or inconclusive findings. Classification can change as more observations emerge; the patient is not a permanent label.

assessment.title: Monitor function and neurological status
assessment.body: Reassess walking, sitting, bending, leg symptoms and relevant neurological findings. An improvement at the spine with new distal weakness is not success. Progressive neurologic loss requires medical assessment.

application.title: 1. Draw a symptom map
application.body: Have the patient show the current location and boundaries of back and leg symptoms. Choose one daily-task baseline such as tolerable standing, walking or sitting, and note symptom behavior before any loading trial.

application.title: 2. Screen for serious problems
application.body: Clarify red flags, progressive weakness, saddle sensory changes, bladder or bowel dysfunction, systemic illness and relevant trauma. These findings demand appropriately escalated medical assessment rather than a routine movement classification.

application.title: 3. Test a hypothesis with appropriate movement
application.body: A trained MDT clinician selects a comfortable repeated movement or sustained position based on the examination—not automatically press-ups. Observe both the during-test and after-test symptom distribution, using caution with high irritability.

application.title: 4. Identify a pattern
application.body: Look for a repeatable change in pain location, movement and function. Centralization, directional preference, end-range pain only or sustained-loading effects suggest different branches of reasoning; uncertain responses may remain mechanically inconclusive.

application.title: 5. Select an individualized strategy
application.body: If a useful directional response is confirmed, guide a manageable self-exercise dose, functional exposure and education. Reassess the patient's ability to carry it out independently. Manual overpressure or more advanced forces are not default requirements.

application.title: 6. Recheck and modify across visits
application.body: Compare the symptom map, most distal symptoms, range and target activity over time. If new neurological signs emerge or the pattern worsens, review the plan and seek appropriate referral. The exercise direction is a provisional tool, not a lifelong identity.

caseStudy.scene: A commuter reports pain into the calf after sitting. 'My back has a mailing list,' he says, 'and the calf gets every message.' The clinician notes a baseline of ten comfortable minutes of walking and the location of the most distant symptoms.
caseStudy.findings: Screening does not identify red flags. A carefully selected repeated loading strategy is tested; the calf symptom becomes less prominent while the back still aches. The therapist documents the shift and checks the response after standing and walking.
caseStudy.decision: The clinician considers a directional preference but does not declare a disc 'back in place.' They explain symptom location, fit the movement to tolerance and give the patient an easy way to monitor both leg symptoms and walking ability.
caseStudy.twist: At the next visit the patient says the back still hurts sometimes but walking has improved and the calf symptom is less frequent. The less dramatic symptom can be the more meaningful outcome. If instead new weakness appeared, the entire plan would change.
caseStudy.finish: A progressive self-management program and periodic re-evaluation follow. If classification stops fitting the symptom behavior, the clinician changes direction rather than forcing the patient into a favorite category.

worldDeep.dose: There is no safe universal repetition count or direction that defines McKenzie care. Some patients require small repeated-movement tests, others sustained positions, modifications or referral. Instruction, dose and progression follow classification, irritability and clinician training.
worldDeep.caution: Do not continue provocative movements with progressive weakness, escalating distal neurological symptoms, saddle anesthesia or bowel/bladder changes; urgent assessment may be required. Avoid diagnosing a displaced disc from centralization or attributing every back pain presentation to derangement.

evidence.known: MDT is a coherent assessment/classification and self-management approach. Directional preference and centralization are recognized clinical phenomena. The method has research for selected musculoskeletal presentations, but results vary by population and comparator.
evidence.unknown: A favorable repeated-movement response does not prove a particular disc reduction mechanism or that extension is superior for everyone. An initial in-session change is not the same as sustained benefit for a person with complex symptoms.
evidence.communication: 'We will test how your symptoms respond to specific movements, then choose a strategy you can manage yourself. The important sign is whether symptoms become more manageable in daily life—not whether one exercise looks famous.'

worldDeep.memoryHook: MDT is a compass for movement response, not a prescription for everybody to do press-ups.

checks.question: A patient's calf symptom decreases while central back pain remains; what is worth documenting?
checks.answer: Track the distal-to-proximal symptom behavior, after-effects, neurologic status and function. A centralizing pattern can be relevant, but it does not prove a disc has moved.

checks.question: When a patient reports end-range pain consistently without directional improvement, which MDT logic deserves consideration?
checks.answer: A dysfunction pattern may be considered in context. The clinician also checks other differential diagnoses and does not force a derangement classification.
